title: 眼儿媚·萍乡道中乍晴
title_en: Yan Er Mei: Sudden Clear Skies on the Road at Pingxiang
author: 范成大

text_note.zh: 语料只题词牌“眼儿媚”。这首词原有小序：“萍乡道中乍晴，卧舆中困甚，小憩柳塘。”通行本多用小序开头几个字作题目。
text_note.en: The corpus gives only the tune name. The ci has a short preface: "On the road at Pingxiang the sky suddenly cleared. Lying in my sedan chair I felt very drowsy, and rested a while by a willow pond." Common editions use its first words as the title.

readings.zh: 泄泄：舒缓、慢悠悠的样子，读 yì yì，不读 xiè xiè。
readings.en: yì yì: slow and easy, read yì, not xiè (to leak).

readings.zh: 欲皱还休：想要起皱又停下了。“还”是“又、却”的意思，读 hái。
readings.en: yù zhòu hái xiū: about to ripple, then stopping again. Here the character means "yet, again", read hái.

glosses.zh: 酣酣：浓浓的、暖洋洋的样子，像喝醉了一样。
glosses.en: hān hān: rich and warm, as if tipsy.

glosses.zh: 日脚：从云缝里照下来的一道道阳光。
glosses.en: rì jiǎo: beams of sunlight slanting down through gaps in the clouds, literally "the sun's feet".

glosses.zh: 紫烟：阳光照着的雾气，带着淡淡的紫色。
glosses.en: zǐ yān: mist lit by the sun, with a faint purple glow.
yán nuǎn: bright and warm. Yán means lovely.

glosses.zh: 破轻裘：暖得连薄皮袄都穿不住了。裘，皮衣。
glosses.en: pò qīng qiú: so warm that even a light fur coat is too much. Qiú is a fur coat.

glosses.zh: 醉人：让人像喝醉了一样。
glosses.en: zuì rén: making people feel drunk.

glosses.zh: 扶头：头昏昏沉沉，要用手撑着。一说“扶头”是一种让人易醉的酒。
glosses.en: fú tóu: the head feels so heavy it must be propped up. One reading says it is the name of a strong wine.

glosses.zh: 春慵：春天里懒洋洋的感觉。慵，懒。
glosses.en: chūn yōng: the lazy feeling of spring. Yōng means lazy, languid.

glosses.zh: 縠纹：水面上细细的波纹，像绉纱上的花纹。縠，一种有皱纹的轻纱。
glosses.en: hú wén: fine ripples on water, like the crinkles on crepe silk. Hú is a light, crinkled gauze.

glosses.zh: 溶溶泄泄：水波慢慢荡漾、舒舒缓缓的样子。
glosses.en: róng róng yì yì: water swaying slowly and gently.

glosses.zh: 欲皱还休：水面好像要起波纹，又平静下来了。
glosses.en: yù zhòu hái xiū: the water seems about to ripple, then settles again.

translation.zh: 暖洋洋的阳光从云缝里照下来，紫色的雾气飘浮着，
translation.en: Warm beams of sun slant through the clouds, and a purple haze floats up,

translation.zh: 晴朗暖和，连薄皮袄都穿不住了。
translation.en: so bright and warm that even a light fur coat is too much.

translation.zh: 花香让人像喝醉了一样，
translation.en: the scent of flowers makes you feel drunk,

translation.zh: 午睡醒来，头还昏昏沉沉的。
translation.en: and after a midday nap your head is still heavy.

translation.zh: 春天这种懒洋洋的心情，正像春天池塘里的水，
translation.en: This lazy spring mood is just like the water of a spring pond,

translation.zh: 泛起一片细细的波纹，带着淡淡的愁。
translation.en: spread with fine ripples, touched with faint sorrow.
The water sways slowly and gently,
the east wind is soft and weak,

translation.zh: 想让水面起皱，却又停下了。
translation.en: about to wrinkle the water, then letting it rest.

background.zh: 范成大在小序里说：在萍乡（今江西萍乡）的路上，天忽然放晴，他躺在轿子里困得不得了，就在一个长着柳树的池塘边歇了一会儿。一般认为这是1173年春天，他从苏州去桂林上任，路过萍乡时写的。
background.en: In his preface Fan Chengda says that on the road at Pingxiang, in today's Jiangxi, the sky suddenly cleared. Lying in his sedan chair he felt terribly sleepy, so he rested a while by a pond lined with willows. It is usually thought he wrote it in the spring of 1173, passing Pingxiang on his way from Suzhou to a new post in Guilin.

author_note.zh: 范成大（1126—1193），号石湖居士，南宋诗人，苏州人。他一生到过很多地方做官，还出使过金国。他很会观察身边的小景物，写农村生活的《四时田园杂兴》最有名。这首词写旅途中的一个春日午后，看得很细。
author_note.en: Fan Chengda (1126–1193), also known as the Lay Buddhist of Stone Lake, was a Southern Song poet from Suzhou. He served in many places during his life and once went as an envoy to the Jin state. He had a sharp eye for small everyday scenes, and his poems on farm life through the seasons are the most famous. This ci captures one spring afternoon on a journey, seen up close.

appreciation.zh: 上片写天气。雨后忽然放晴，阳光一道道照下来，雾气带着紫色，暖得连薄皮袄都嫌热。天色让人困，花香让人醉，午睡起来头还是晕晕的。读着读着，自己好像也要打哈欠了。下片最妙：词人说，春天这种懒懒的、有点说不清的愁，就像池塘里的春水。水面轻轻荡着，东风软得没力气，想吹出波纹，吹了一下又停了。人的心情也是这样，好像有点愁，又愁不起来。把看不见的心情，写成看得见的水波，这个比喻又新又准。
appreciation.en: The first half is about the weather. After rain the sky suddenly clears, beams of sun slant down, the mist glows purple, and it is so warm that even a light fur coat feels hot. The weather makes you sleepy, the flowers make you tipsy, and after a nap your head is still fuzzy. Reading it, you almost want to yawn too. The second half is the cleverest part. The poet says this lazy, hard-to-name spring sadness is like the water in a spring pond. The water sways gently. The east wind is too soft to do much: it starts to make ripples, then stops. His mood is the same: a little sad, but not quite able to be sad. Turning a feeling you cannot see into ripples you can see is a fresh and exact picture.
